reviews.body:
I've owned the SHP9500 (three times), the 9600 (twice), and now the 9500cy.  My preferences for headphones generally speaking - I'm a sucker for soundstage and separation in music.  Love it.

Why do I have ANOTHER pair of SHPs?  I sold my PS5, and have been gaming on a small retro handheld.  No longer hooking up to the TV and my Atom stack, I had to downsize to a headphone that doesn't take much juice to give me the audio experience I want - immersion.
Review format: Use case > Benefit > Comparison to other headphones I have (had)

Use case:

I've been using these for both music on my Shanling m1plus and gaming on my handheld.
Gaming
: Playing something like Final Fantasy XII with these really gives you an idea of where enemies might be offscreen, and what's going on with the rest of your party if you can't see them.  Anyone who has done PVE gaming with the 9500 will tell you it's good, especially for the sub $100 price.
Gaming Benefit: 
Distance, positioning and layering of sound are all top notch.  If you're playing PVP you will find resolution to be the limiting factor, but otherwise they're fantastic for cinematic or story-based single player gaming.

Bonus points for being easy to drive.  My Retroid Pocket 6 can power them to satisfying effect at like 30% volume.
Not many photos of how angled those drivers really are:
Music
: They shine with well-recorded music, especially large orchestral work, acoustic bands or vocal work. They can do rock, if it's not too old and tinny. They can also do some electronica and synthwave, as the midbass and upper bass supply a good amount of warmth despite the subbass not being there for body. Doesn't stop me from listening to Deadmaus with them 

Claire Pelletier's 
Poussière d'Étoiles 
features an ensemble of acoustic instruments backed by some new-age sounding synth, including a sick drum and bass guitar intro that really sets the tone.  From the album 
Murmures d'Histoire, 
which I highly recommend checking out if you like Celtic music... but would like it in French.

The best comparison of music that works and music that doesn’t due to recording quality would be David Bowie’s 
Blackstar
 vs Beck’s 
Modern Guilt
.  
Blackstar
 is a treat end to end, but some of 
Modern Guilt
 feels too thin due to the missing subbass body, and the entire album was recorded a little thin to begin with, so it becomes strident.  Especially on the title track. Or perhaps Anna Ternheim’s 
The Night Visitor
 vs T.Rex’s 
Slider
.   Anna Ternheim's recordings feel real, like you could be in the recording booth with her. That said, what the hell made Marc Bolan equate “dynamically compressed” with “live concert sound?”  It's murder on anything other than a dark, or overly warm and bassy headphone.  A shame because the music rocks.

A perfect song to display the SHP9500cy's abilities is L'Impératrice's 
Danza Marilú.  
The singer's vocals are crisp, though never piercing, the strings are audible and don't meld with the vocals.  The bass guitar is super easy to track, with a satisfying amount of thump.  Conversely, the same band's song 
Love from the Other Side 
has a lot of subbass rumbling around the 2:50 mark, which while easily audible isn't super tactile.  That song is actually a great showcase for imaging and separation with the various layers of vocals.
Music benefit: 
Highly realistic timbre, much like the HD660s2 they’ve replaced.  Instruments like harp or acoustic guitar have a tactile pluck to them, very much full and 3 dimensional. I find these headphones to be extremely light on the head both in weight and clamp force, and for once, the 6k spike that every SHP has doesn't seem to bug me when listening to most music, so hours of listening time are easy to accrue.  Horns will pop more than I like, but I don't listen to Jazz or (much) Wagner, so I'm not bothered.  These are relaxed enough for me to fall asleep while listening.  The drawback, again, is resolution.  Some sounds will get masked if there is a lot going on.  Casual listening, or traveling to see family, these are an easy go to.  Serious listening I'll use my custom Hifimans.

They don’t take much power.  On my Atom 2 amp, 9 o’clock is enough.  On my Shanling m1plus, 30% works and 40% really bangs.
Comparisons:

HE5XX Custom
 - The 5XX simply does everything the 9500cy does, but better.  It digs deeper into the subbass, and has greater control and definition from top to bottom. Separation, imaging and texture is all superior.  Instruments don't get masked by percussion, especially in the case of kick drum/large toms/bass guitar (Soundgarden's "Fourth of July" bass guitar is EASY to track on the 5XX, but becomes difficult on the 9500cy).  Soundstage also goes to the 5XX, while timbre goes to the Philips.
HD660S2 
- I sold my S2 after getting the 9500cy.  Tonality wise they are SUPER similar, both portray music in a very REAL, believable way, though the Sennheisers were the final word in resolution.  Treble was just about the same in terms of volume, but certainly more delicate on the S2.  There is more airiness in the 9500, but also it can be ever so slightly more sharp.  But only just.  The 9500cy wins regarding soundstage and imaging, hands down.  Sennheisers have more bass extension, but less midbass elevation, making the Philips sound warmer and more satisfying on most tracks.  The trade off for convenience in ease to drive is really inferior resolution, by a large margin.  Is it worth trading down?  I thought it was, but only for my use case.  I love the 660S2, just couldn't really use it the way I wanted to anymore.
ATH-R50x 
- The R50x was WAY more treble forward than the Philips, and the midrange was harder to hear.  Also, despite the featherlike weight of the R50x, it was still less comfortable as the pads were so thin your ears are guaranteed to touch the inside of the headphone.  Better resolution than the Philips, though.  I'd still take the Philips over the Audiotechnica time and again.
OG 9500/9600 - 
The 9500cy is almost identical to the OG 9500, but with fuller bass and smoother treble.  It doesn’t share many qualities with the 9600, whose midrange was a bit subdued and bass was wooly and overwhelming at times.  I didn't really enjoy the 9600, despite giving it a try twice.  I suspect that The Freddie's superiority comes down to the new fabric they've used, with a tighter weave and smoother texture.  The Freddie is the best of the three.
K371 
- "How can I compare these to a closed-back?" you ask.  I won't, save to say that both headphones sound 
realistic
 despite significantly different tuning characteristics.  Their profiles lean in opposite directions, but it seems to me that both of their midranges have significant overlap, so vocals and fundamentals of instruments sound correct.  These two headphones compliment each other extremely well. If you wanted only one open back and one closed back, for reasonable, average person money, these headphones are perfect.  *** I use Dekoni's velour pads on the K371, which eliminated any seal issues I had while wearing glasses.  A must have, IMO.
A great pairing:
SUMMARY

They're good.  The “baby hd6xx” moniker continues to apply, here.  They feature a small, angled driver in an open back chassis, so profound subbass was never really going to be part of the equation. They make up for this shortcoming, and average resolution, with a big soundstage, great imaging, realistic timbre, and a comfortable fit.

There are definitely worse ways to spend $70-90.  Grab yourself a KBEar 3.5mm cable to replace the janky piece of garbage it came with for roughly $12, and you have a solid casual listening/gaming headphone for under $100. Recommended.
